summary: Specifies version 1.0 of the Token Binding protocol, which lets client and server create long-lived, uniquely identifiable TLS bindings that span multiple sessions and connections. Applications can use them to cryptographically bind security tokens to the TLS layer.

eli5.summary: A ticket works only if it carries your own fingerprint. If a thief steals the ticket, it will not work for them.

questions: how to bind tokens to tls
how does token binding stop token theft
what is a token binding id
which key types does token binding support
subtitle: A way to tie login cookies and tokens to a key that never leaves the user's device, so stolen tokens stop working.

tldr.problem: Bearer tokens such as HTTP cookies and OAuth tokens work for anyone who holds them, so attackers export them from a user's machine and replay them to impersonate the user.
tldr.mechanism: The client makes a key pair per server, proves it holds the private key on every TLS connection by signing exported keying material, and the server puts the matching Token Binding ID into the tokens it issues.
tldr.outcome: A stolen bound token is useless on another machine unless the attacker also exports the private key, which is hard if the key sits in secure hardware.

today: RFC 8471 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It notes that it deals with TLS 1.2, whose RFC 5246 was obsoleted by RFC 8446, and that TLS 1.3 is handled in a separate document.

sections.title: Stolen Tokens and the Binding Idea
sections.content:
Servers hand out security tokens such as HTTP cookies and OAuth tokens (RFC 6749). These are bearer tokens: whoever holds one gets access to the protected resource. Attackers take advantage by exporting tokens from a user's connections or machines, presenting them to servers and impersonating authenticated users.

Token Binding prevents this by cryptographically binding application tokens to the underlying TLS layer. To export and replay a bound token, the attacker must also be able to use the client's private key, which is hard if the key is protected, for example generated in a secure hardware module.
sections.eli5: Normally a ticket works for whoever is holding it, so a thief can use a stolen one. Token Binding writes your fingerprint on the ticket, so it only works when you show up.

sections.title: How a Token Binding Works
sections.content:
A user agent generates a private-public key pair per target server, possibly inside a secure hardware module such as a Trusted Platform Module. It gives the public key to the server and proves possession of the private key on every TLS connection to that server. The proof is a signature over the Exported Keying Material (EKM) of the TLS connection (RFC 5705).

The public key travels in a structure called the Token Binding ID. Bindings are long-lived: they span many TLS connections and sessions between one client and one server. When the server issues a token, it includes the client's Token Binding ID or a cryptographic hash of it. When a token comes back, the server checks that the ID inside matches the ID established on the current connection, and rejects the token on a mismatch.

Version 1.0 is negotiated during the TLS handshake with the extension from RFC 8472, without extra round trips. The protocol itself is a single message, sent by the client with its application data. RFC 8473 covers carrying that message in HTTP.
sections.eli5: You give the shop a lock once and keep the key. Every time you visit you show you still have the key, and the shop only honors tickets made for your lock.

sections.title: The Token Binding Message
sections.content:
The message is a TokenBindingMessage: a series of TokenBinding structures. Each has a tokenbinding_type, a tokenbindingid, a signature and optional extensions. The client MUST send the message if Token Binding was negotiated, MUST NOT send it otherwise, and MUST put it in its first application protocol message. It MAY send more in later messages to prove possession of additional keys.

There are two types. provided_token_binding (0) establishes a binding when connecting to a server. referred_token_binding (1) is used when requesting tokens meant for a different server, for example when a user agent talks to an Identity Provider about a token for a Relying Party. Unknown types MUST be ignored.

The Token Binding ID holds the key parameters identifier, the key length in bytes and the public key. The key parameters defined are rsa2048_pkcs1.5 (0), rsa2048_pss (1) and ecdsap256 (2). Implementations SHOULD hand IDs to applications as opaque byte sequences.
sections.eli5: The message is a note that says what kind of binding this is, shows the public half of your key, and carries a signature only you could make.

sections.title: Keys and Signatures
sections.content:
For RSA, the ID carries the modulus and exponent of a 2048-bit public key in big-endian format. For ecdsap256 it carries the X and Y coordinates of a Curve P-256 key, each an unsigned 32-byte integer. RSA signatures use RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 or RSASSA-PSS with SHA256. For PSS, MGF1 with SHA256 MUST be used and the salt length MUST equal 32 bytes. ECDSA signatures are a pair of 32-byte integers, R followed by S.

The signature covers the concatenation of the token binding type, the key parameters value and the EKM from the current TLS connection. The EKM is obtained with the exporter label EXPORTER-Token-Binding, no context value and a length of 32 bytes. Because the EKM is unique to the connection, a signature from one connection does not verify on another.

TLS 1.2 and earlier support renegotiation, which creates a new master secret and a new EKM on the same connection. The signature MUST use the EKM from the master secret that produced the keys encrypting the record carrying the message. Specifications for application protocols may prohibit renegotiation with Token Binding, or must define how to find the matching EKM.
sections.eli5: The signature is like signing your name on a card that has today's secret code printed on it. The code changes every visit, so an old signed card is worthless.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
The client MUST include at least one TokenBinding. For a provided binding, the key parameters MUST match those negotiated. The client MUST generate and store keys in a manner that prevents key export, and the scope of a key MUST NOT be broader than the scope of the tokens, so cooperating servers cannot link user identities. A referred binding is built from the Token Binding ID used with the Relying Party, signed with the key for that party over the EKM of the connection to the Identity Provider.

The server MUST reject all bindings if Token Binding was not negotiated. For a provided binding it MUST check that the algorithm (including the curve for ECDSA) and key length match what was negotiated. It MUST reject the binding if the message has no TokenBinding or any signature is invalid, and it MUST ignore unknown extensions. Referred bindings may use different parameters. A rejected binding means any bound tokens on that connection MUST also be rejected, with an application-specific effect such as failed requests or re-authentication.

How tokens are bound is up to the application: embed the ID or its hash in the token, or keep a database mapping tokens to IDs. A bound token on a connection without a binding, or with a different ID, MUST be rejected. Whether to accept plain bearer tokens is application policy.
sections.eli5: The visitor has to show the right key, and the shop has to check it. If the check fails, the shop refuses every ticket tied to that key.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Malware inside the user agent can still replay bound tokens, and that may be undetectable to a server. Exporting tokens to other machines requires exporting the private keys, so keys SHOULD be strongly protected, ideally in hardware that prevents export. Bound tokens need integrity protection so an attacker cannot strip or swap the ID. Cooperating clients can still share a bound token plus its key, and applications that share tokens (for single sign-on) must share keys only within the same group.

Negotiation MUST use a downgrade-resistant mechanism, such as the TLS extension of RFC 8472. Because of the triple handshake attack, Token Binding MUST NOT be negotiated with TLS 1.2 or older unless the extended master secret (RFC 7627) and renegotiation indication (RFC 5746) extensions are also negotiated.

For privacy, IDs are never sent in clear text and the user can reset them at any time, for example when clearing cookies. In a private browsing mode, applications SHOULD use fresh keys and delete them on exit, or not negotiate Token Binding. A server can use tokens and IDs to track clients, so key lifetime and scope should match any limits placed on tokens.
sections.eli5: A thief who also steals your key can still cheat, so keep the key somewhere it cannot be copied. The fingerprint can also be wiped away whenever you want, so you cannot be followed around forever.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: The RFC creates a "Token Binding Protocol" registry with three subregistries: Key Parameters, Types and Extensions, each using the Specification Required policy with values 0 to 255. The initial entries are the three key parameters and two types listed above. No extensions are registered initially; attestation, proof that a key is hardware bound, is mentioned as one possible future use. It also registers the TLS exporter label EXPORTER-Token-Binding.
sections.eli5: It starts a public list of the kinds of keys and bindings allowed, so new kinds can be added later in an orderly way.

items.label: rsa2048_pss
items.desc: 2048-bit RSA with RSASSA-PSS, MGF1 with SHA256, salt length 32 bytes.

items.label: ecdsap256
items.desc: ECDSA on Curve P-256 with SHA256.

items.title: Key parameters
items.text: Which key type and signature algorithm are in use.

items.title: EKM
items.text: 32 bytes exported from the current TLS connection with label EXPORTER-Token-Binding.
